title: Object infixes: ninakupenda in one word
goal: Say who receives the action without a separate word — phoning, asking for help, passing on greetings — by slipping one extra slot into the middle of the verb.
bekal: where they go: subject + tense + **object** + root
object infixes for things, which mean "that one, the one we mentioned"

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kwenye simu
dialogs.intro: Evening. Amina calls Budi because she left something on campus.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Hello? Budi? Can you hear me?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ndiyo, ninakusikia vizuri. Habari za jioni?
lines.id: Yes, I can hear you clearly. Good evening, how are you?
lines.literal: yes, I-am-you-hearing well. news of evening?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Fine. Could you help me with something?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Nimesahau kitabu changu chuoni. Unaweza kukichukua?
lines.id: I left my book on campus. Could you get it?
lines.literal: I-have-forgotten book of-mine at-campus. you-can to-it-take?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ninakiona sasa hivi, kiko mezani. Nikilete lini?
lines.id: I can see it right now, it's on the table. When should I bring it?
lines.literal: I-am-it-seeing now this, it-is at-table. I-should-it-bring when?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Tomorrow morning. You'll find me at the bus stop.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Okay. I'll wait for you at eight sharp.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Thanks so much! You always help me.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hakuna shida. Sisi ni marafiki, tunasaidiana.
lines.id: No problem. We're friends, we help each other.
lines.literal: there-is-no problem. we are friends, we-are-each-other-helping.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nisalimie mama! Tutaonana kesho, usiku mwema.
lines.id: Say hi to your mom for me! See you tomorrow, good night.
lines.literal: greet-for-me mother! we-will-each-other-see tomorrow, night good.

notes: **Kusalimia means to pass on greetings to someone.** *Anakusalimia* = she says hi to you; *Nisalimie mama* = say hi to your mom for me. Sending greetings is a strong custom in East Africa — almost every phone call ends with greetings to the whole household.

**Sasa hivi means both "just now" and "in a moment".** Past and future squeezed into one phrase. If someone says *ninakuja sasa hivi*, get ready to wait — and look back at the note on time in unit 10.

**Kila wakati means "every time; always".** *Kila* works just like "every": *kila siku* (every day), *kila mtu* (everyone), *kila mahali* (everywhere). It's one of the few words that comes **before** its noun.

**Usiku mwema is "good night" when parting.** To greet someone in the evening, use *habari za usiku*. Its partner is *lala salama* (sleep well — literally "sleep in safety"), said to someone going to bed.
**Marafiki is the plural of rafiki.** Because it's a loanword, its plural takes *ma-*, not *wa-* — even though it means people. Likewise *madaktari*, *madereva*, *maaskari*.

grammars.title: Object infixes: who it's done to
body: The Swahili verb has one more slot, and it sits right in the middle: **subject + tense + object + root**.
after: For **people**, the infix is almost always **required**, even when the name is given: *Ninamwona Amina* (I see Amina) — not *ninaona Amina*. Infix and name go together, and that's exactly what sounds natural.
The infix *-m-* becomes **-mw-** before a vowel: *ninamwona* (I see him), *ninamwuliza* (I ask her), but *ninampenda* (I like him) and *ninamsaidia* (I help her).

Object infixes work with every tense slot and with the *-e* form too: *nilikuona* (I saw you), *nitakusubiri* (I'll wait for you), *nimemwona* (I've seen him), *unisaidie* (please help me), *usinisahau* (don't forget me).

grammars.title: Things as objects
body: Things can be objects too, and the infix **follows the noun class** — it sounds just like the subject prefix you already know. The difference: for things the infix is **optional**, and using it means "that one, the one we've been talking about".
after: Compare these two: *Ninanunua kitabu* (I'm buying a book — any book) and *Ninakinunua kitabu* (I'm buying that book — the one we just saw). The infix works like a "that" stuck onto the verb.
Some verbs **always** take an infix because their meaning calls for a specific object: *kukumbuka* (to remember), *kupenda* (to like), *kuchukia* (to hate) — almost never used without one.

The ending **-ana** you met in *tutaonana* is this page's twin: instead of adding an object, it says the two sides do it to each other. *Kusaidia* (to help) → *kusaidiana* (to help each other); *kupenda* → *kupendana*; *kuona* → *kuonana*; *kujua* → *kujuana* (to know each other).

blocks.text: Notice that nearly all of these use the *-e* form from unit 14 with *-ni-* inside. The build: *u* (you) + *ni* (me) + root + *-e* → *unisaidie*, which in speech is often shortened to just *nisaidie*.
*Ninakukumbuka* is for missing someone, while plain *Nakumbuka* means "I remember". One small infix separates memory from longing.

sections.title: Kwenye simu — on the phone in Swahili

head: Kiswahili
English
rows: Call me when you get there.

blocks.text: In East Africa, phone credit is *salio* and a data bundle is *bandeli* or *kifurushi*. Sentences you'll need at the airtime kiosk: *Naomba salio ya elfu tano* (credit for five thousand, please) and *Nataka bandeli ya wiki* (I want a weekly bundle).

A distinctive habit: *kupiga miss* — calling and hanging up straight away so the other person calls back. It isn't rude, just a credit-saving trick everyone understands, and it has its own slang name: *kubipu*.

items: Could you help me a little?
